Thanks for adding these. Two things on `cf33b01a9`:

The four delete tests check `table.newScan().planFiles()` with `doesNotThrowAnyException()`, but `planFiles()` is lazy. `ManifestGroup.plan()` builds the `DeleteFileIndex` right away, but data manifests are only read when the iterable is consumed, so the step that matches deletes to data files by partition value never runs. body:
Getting a bit long, hard to read...
Shall we refactor the documentation a bit

```suggestion
- The index is **reused across triggers and restored on failover** while it matches the head of the target branch: the head is the snapshot the index was built from, or the converter's own commit for the last planned staging snapshot directly on top of it. Each cycle applies its staging snapshot's changes to the index, so consecutive conversions do not rebuild it.
- Otherwise the next trigger **rebuilds the index** from the target branch head, reading the equality columns of every live data file. This happens:
    - on cold start without a checkpoint, and on the first trigger after restoring state written by an older Iceberg version
    - after any other commit on the target branch, e.g. compaction, external writes, rollback, or replace-main (see *Concurrent commits on the target branch* below)
    - after restoring a checkpoint that predates the latest conversion commit
    - when the last planned conversion did not commit
    - when an earlier rebuild did not finish
```
title: Review comment on apache/iceberg#18674 (docs/docs/flink-maintenance.md)

body:
Might just remove the first sentence after the changes above.

```suggestion
- On restart, the planner rediscovers its position by walking the target branch for the marker property `equality-convert-staging-snapshot` written by the committer. If that marker is no longer reachable on the target branch (target was rolled back, replace-main'ed, or the marker snapshot was expired) the planner fails and requires manual intervention.
```

@huaxingao Thanks, you're right. I tried the example on the 4.2 tests (MoR UPDATE, with the concurrent change committed right before the UPDATE commits, same setup as the tests in this PR). With the current check the UPDATE fails; with this PR it commits.

Without a subquery on the same table, the UPDATE's result depends only on rows that match its condition. All of those are in data files it modifies, so the narrowed check still catches every concurrent delete that changes the result. Concurrent inserts are still checked by `validateNoConflictingDataFiles()` under SERIALIZABLE. The difference is only for UPDATEs whose subquery reads other rows of the same table, and the write can't tell those apart: it only gets the command and the target scan's filter.

body:
The `1.10.x` branch currently uses Guava `33.4.8-jre`, which is within the affected version range for CVE-2026-102554 (versions earlier than `33.7.2`).

This vulnerability affects Java deserialization of certain Guava collection implementations, potentially leading to excessive memory allocation and denial of service.

Since Iceberg bundles and relocates Guava, users consuming the `1.10.x` release line would continue to receive the affected Guava version unless we upgrade it.

The purpose of this PR is to backport the Guava security fix to the `1.10.x` maintenance branch, allowing users to receive the updated dependency without having to move to a newer Iceberg minor version.

Additionally, this change replaces the affected Guava `Queues` usages with equivalent JDK collection implementations to ensure compatibility with Shadow JAR minimization.

body:
@pvary
> What are the expectation of the time for the commits?

Well below the commit interval. Our target is about 3 minutes from a change to its visibility. With a commit interval of 60 to 90 s, the conversion should take at most about 80 s, or about 40 s so that one retry still fits.

> Is a worst case full read acceptable?

Not on large tables, I think. When the changes are spread over the key space, every commit reads the key column of the whole table. Our two largest CDC tables are unpartitioned, with about 150 to 160 data files and 1.7 and 2.4 billion rows. Amoro already reads all of these files after each commit to turn the equality deletes into position deletes. It runs one task per data file in parallel, and still takes 14 s and 43 s. I haven't measured the conversion on our storage yet, but doing that in one coordinator on every commit is too expensive.

So I'd document in part 2 that the conversion suits tables where the key filter or the partition spec prunes most data files, such as increasing keys with changes on recent rows. Tables with changes spread over many rows need an index behind `KeyPositionResolver`, as a follow-up.

body:
The specification states that a write-default expression is evaluated for any record written after the field was added, provided the writer does not supply a value. This defines which records receive a default, but leaves the evaluation frequency of non-deterministic functions ambiguous: once per row, per write operation, or per file/commit.

For example, ANSI SQL (and Spark) evaluate current_timestamp() once per statement, so a batch "INSERT INTO t SELECT ..." writing 10M rows to a table with a created_at TIMESTAMP write-default of current_timestamp() would assign the same timestamp to every row. In contrast, a streaming sink might evaluate the expression per record or per checkpoint, producing different timestamps across rows. Furthermore, after checkpoint replay, re-emitted records could receive new values, making the write non-idempotent. Consequently, the same table metadata could produce different results across engines. To avoid this ambiguity, I suggest explicitly specifying that non-deterministic functions in write-default expressions must be evaluated at most once per write operation, consistent with SQL statement-level semantics. Alternatively, if per-record evaluation i […]

body:
```suggestion
Schemas are matched by column name. The table schemas are checked starting with the current schema, then from newest to oldest. A table schema which matches the record exactly is preferred over one which needs a conversion (for example `Integer` to `Long`), so a record which has the shape of an older table schema is written with that schema, even if it would also fit the current one. The exceptions are older table schemas which use a column name that belongs to a different column in the current schema, for example after a column was dropped and added again, or renamed and its name reused. Data written with such a schema is stored under column IDs which queries on the current schema do not read, so these schemas are only used when the record fits no other table schema, not even with a conversion. In that case the affected values are not visible through the current schema.
```

body: Right, released clients don't send it. Today the Java client only sets a User-Agent when `rest.client.user-agent` is configured, so servers see the Apache HttpClient default (they can still identify old Java clients from the `X-Client-Version` header). The spec can't change what's already shipped, which is why the advisory rules say servers SHOULD NOT reject a request whose header is absent, incomplete, or malformed. The MUST is for clients that follow this format from now on, so a server can always rely on the library token being there. With a SHOULD, it couldn't rely on it even for new clients. This is also the wording the vote passed on. The client changes that add the token (Java, Python, Go, Rust) are ready and will go out once this merges.

body: manuzhang asked which status code a refusing server should return (https://github.com/apache/iceberg/pull/17727#discussion_r4290683598). 400 is the standard client-error response. The Java client raises it as a BadRequestException with the server's message and doesn't retry it, so naming the refused version tells the user what to upgrade. Other codes send the wrong signal: 403 reads as a permissions problem, and this header must not be used for authorization; 409 is a commit conflict, which the Java client retries. It's a SHOULD, so a server can still pick a different code.

Logical checks that operating data has not changed:
- Data files were added

- Data files are missing

Physical checks for reference integrity

body: I think that `timestamptz` makes more sense than `timestamp`. Timestamp with time zone represents a point in time that will be shown to users in the SQL session time zone. If we were to use timestamp without time zone, the only difference would be that the time would be shown to all users the same way. In either case, the value is stored as some offset from the unix epoch. I think showing the value in the session time zone is what users expect so we should use `timestamptz`.

body:
This is wider than `Evaluator`. `SparkV2Filters` notes that Iceberg expressions are 2-valued (it rewrites `NOT IN` to `notNull && notIn`), and `StrictEvalVisitor` also treats `notEq` / `notIn` as matching all-null files. Changing only `Evaluator` would make it disagree with the metrics evaluators.

Should expressions become 3-valued across the evaluators, or stay 2-valued and be documented? Happy to do either.

Did have a discussion on this with @pvary : It's not really sophisticated to have such a switch on the exact type of the `ScanTask` here. We believe that the `ScanTask` implementations themselves should be able to tell us, what are their referenced files if there are any. That would be the right level of abstraction.

As an implementation what we have in mind is to have some interface like `HasReferencedFiles` with a single function `referencedFiles()` returning a collection of `ContentFile`s.
Then here in the decryptor we can iterate the list of `ScanTasks` verify that they implement the new interface (throw if not) and ask them to give us their referenced files.

You are right, I was rushing things a bit here - the design doc was recommending this change, but now I think it shouldn't.

I'll amend the design doc and revert the changes here and make the bearer manager strictly opt-in. We'll keep inferring `oauth2` (v1) from `token`, as today.

Let's just keep in mind though that the new OAuth2 manager v2 (#18756) will _not_ handle `token`. To upgrade, users of `token` will have 2 options:

- Upgrade to `oauth2` v2 and provide valid OAuth2 credentials instead of a raw token.
- Upgrade to `bearer` and keep using raw tokens as before.

I'm considering closing this implementation in favor of documenting the limitation and a verified workaround (docs PR to follow). #18748 stays open. Here is a summary:

**Design.** When every partition spec is partitioned only by equality fields, the writer also emits each equality delete for every older spec it saw at startup, as long as the key column types match. An unpartitioned older spec gets a global delete. Checkpoint state keeps one delete manifest per spec (serializer v3), and a delete that cancels an insert from the same checkpoint stays a position delete. This fixes deletes against rows committed in earlier checkpoints for those tables, but every variant runs into a tension between covering older specs, read cost, and the spec lifecycle:

- **Read cost.** For unpartitioned → bucketed evolution, every upsert adds a global equality delete. That adds delete-processing work across all partitions, and as long as those deletes are emitted and live, they keep the old spec referenced. Skipping specs that no longer hold data needs a liveness check in the writer, which loads metadata in every subtask and races with concurrent commits.

There is no common parent of `DataFile`, `DeleteFile` and `ColumnFile` that we could use here, unfortunately. We have a couple of ways to solve this:
1) In the future if we introduce something like an `EncryptedFile` we could introduce a variation that returns the common interface, but for now we don't have anything like that. This might be a long-term solution.
2) We could adapt/wrap a `ColumnFile` to seem like a `ContentFile` and then we can return them as part of the list. Might seem a nasty workaround, I probably wouldn't be in favor of this option.
3) Technically, `ContentFile` contains the column files. In the decryptor we can get the `ColumnFile`s if a file is a `DataFile` instance.

I think I'd prefer 3) because then there is a single place where we change the code for column file coverage and we get it everywhere, where the decryptor is used.

About the other question: I have considered that option too. What I wanted to avoid is to have a default implementation that compiles and runs but then silently misses some files in case of an implementation that doesn't override it. > @MonkeyCanCode thanks for confirming that at least #18378 fixes the original issue. The reason you're seeing this particular stack trace is because we register the `FileIO` instance to be closed in `RESTSessionCatalog` but the `RESTSessionCatalog` itself is never closed, hence we're leaking `FileIO` instances there. We're still closing them but we're issuing a WARN msg to tell users that this is a resource leak. The same is true for the executor used in `RESTMetricsReporter` as its closing is tied to `RESTSessionCatalog` being closed.

Thanks @nastra, that makes sense. To clarify the direction for the remaining part:
1. Is closing the catalog the preferred fix (https://github.com/apache/spark/pull/59952) plus SparkCatalog/SparkSessionCatalog passing close() through (this PR)?
2. Separately, would you accept letting the metrics executor's idle thread exit (allowCoreThreadTimeOut, no inherited thread-locals)? I tested it on top of https://github.com/apache/iceberg/pull/18378, and released Spark Connect sessions are no longer retained even without catalog close. The FileIO warning remains in that case, as expected.

Indeed we don't carry over any defaults from the catalog properties, so if the `SessionContext` does not contain a token endpoint, but contains other OAuth2 properties, the default catalog internal token endpoint would be used.

Why I think it's generally not a good idea to merge catalog properties with context properties: consider the following setup:

* Catalog properties:
  ```properties
  rest.auth.oauth2.issuer-url=issuer1
  rest.auth.oauth2.client-id=client1
  rest.auth.oauth2.client-secret=secret1
  rest.auth.oauth2.resource=resource1
  ```

* Context properties (note no client secret, maybe hinting at a public client):
  ```properties
  rest.auth.oauth2.issuer-url=issuer2
  rest.auth.oauth2.client-id=client2
  rest.auth.oauth2.audience=audience2
  ```

If we blindly merge the two, we'd get:

```properties
rest.auth.oauth2.token-endpoint=issuer2
rest.auth.oauth2.client-id=client2
rest.auth.oauth2.client-secret=secret1
rest.auth.oauth2.resource=resource1
rest.auth.oauth2.audience=audience2
```

Which is almost certainly a wrong setup.

I have asked an AI to collect the possible failure scenarios, and distributed them based on whether they can be reried-or-not.

Transient: retrying the same delta works
- Storage throttling or outages: S3/GCS/ADLS 503 or 429 errors last longer than the FileIO retries.
- Credential refresh hiccup: an STS/IMDS timeout, or the REST catalog's refresh endpoint is briefly down.
- Replication lag: a replica doesn't have a just-committed manifest list yet, so the read returns 404.
- Catalog outage: table.refresh() fails before the delta even starts.

Already ends in a rebuild
- Snapshot expiry by another engine: it deletes manifest lists mid-read, and on the next trigger the walk breaks and the planner rebuilds.

Never succeeds, though a rebuild at the head would (the delta is stuck)
- Leaked equality delete, later cleaned up: validateTargetDeleteFiles fails on every trigger.
- Lost metadata of an older snapshot: a lifecycle rule, cleanup script or orphan-file removal deleted a manifest list the head no longer uses.
- Corrupt manifest from a buggy writer: it was later replaced by a manifest merge or rewrite, but the delta still reads it.

Reproduced with DuckDB 2.0.0's Iceberg extension as the client, on `apache/iceberg-rest-fixture:latest` built from `b0df3ca`, using the JDBC catalog on SQLite.

Two `MERGE` statements committed through `/v1/transactions/commit`, with a proxy releasing both commit requests at the same moment. Both returned 204, and one write was lost in 12 of 12 rounds:
- guarded on empty `main`, same new row (4 of 4)
- guarded on an existing `main` snapshot, different new rows (4 of 4)
- guarded on an existing `main` snapshot, update to the same row (4 of 4)

So this also affects commits on a table with existing data, including appends of unrelated rows, and not only a guard on empty `main`. The catalog log showed the same sequence: `Cannot commit ... metadata location has changed`, `Retrying task after failure: sleepTimeMs=100`, `Nothing to commit.`

When the second commit was released after the first had finished, it got the expected 409.

For comparison, AWS S3 Tables with the same client lost no writes in 36 rounds of concurrent merges.

Suggested text changes -
**In Column Files**

A column file stores the fields listed in its `field_ids`. A listed struct includes all fields nested in it. In this section, a struct _contains_ a field if the field is nested in the struct at any depth.

Each ID in `field_ids` must identify a field in the schema of the file it modifies, or a row lineage field required by [Writing Column Files](#writing-column-files). The schema of a data file is the table schema. The schema of a leaf manifest is the tracked file schema. Fields nested in a list or map must not be listed in `field_ids`.

If a column file of an entry lists a struct, no other column file of that entry can list a field that the struct contains.

**In Writing Column Files**

The added column files must list each field that the update changes, or a struct that contains that field. If an update changes whether a struct is null, the update changes that struct.

+1, I think these rules are right and we need them. The current text has two problems with structs:

1. Reading: L1811 says a listed struct includes its nested fields, but L1840 only reads a field from a column file if its own ID is listed. So with `field_ids: [2]`, `customer.name` (3) would be read from the data file.

2. Writing: if column file A lists `[3]` and a later update adds column file B with `[2]`, L1833 only removes ID 2, so A keeps `[3]`. The reader then reads the old `name` from A. Your change to also remove the fields a listed struct contains fixes this.

One small suggestion: could we put "no other column file of that entry can list a field that the struct contains" next to the rule in the `column_files` field section ("A field ID may appear in `field_ids` of at most one column file")? Then the overlap rules are in one place.

I'd like to take ownership of investigating and preparing a fix for this issue, if no one is already actively working on it.

The reported race condition in `JdbcLockFactory.initializeLockTables()` appears to occur when multiple Flink maintenance operators concurrently check for the lock table's existence and attempt to create it.

My proposed approach is to:

1. Add regression coverage for concurrent lock-table initialization.
2. Handle the table-already-exists race safely by verifying the table's existence after a conflicting creation attempt.
3. Preserve proper exception handling for genuine JDBC connection failures and other SQL errors.
4. Run the relevant Flink maintenance tests before submitting a PR.

I'm planning to work on this shortly and would be happy to submit a focused PR referencing #18797.

@maintainers, please let me know if there is a preferred approach or if someone is already working on a fix. I'd appreciate being assigned to this issue if appropriate, to help avoid duplicate efforts.

Thanks!

Hi @mxm @pvary, could you review this? It documents #18748 and a workaround validated through stop-with-savepoint → spec change → rewrite → rebuild and restore, on main and a non-main branch.

The prototype fix in #18747 writes deletes across historical specs, but requires a serializer-version change. In addition, it only supports partitioning based on equality fields and still misses Dynamic Sink changes within one checkpoint. Given that complexity, limited coverage, and v4’s prohibition on new equality-delete files, I’m leaning toward landing these docs rather than pursuing #18747.

As a follow-up, I’d suggest a startup check that rejects upsert/CDC writers using a partitioned spec when the target branch contains data files under another spec. That would turn existing mismatches into an explicit error instead of silent incorrect results. Runtime spec changes would need separate handling. Does that direction make sense?

Thanks @adiranjan25. A predicate-side helper that leaves the bound ordering alone is the fix I had in mind, so I'll review here instead of sending a second patch.

Two places still compare with the plain comparator, so `x = 0.0` can still miss `-0.0` rows:

Since it's in the same module, I'd fix it in this PR.
2. `ParquetDictionaryRowGroupFilter` in `parquet`. `eq` and `notEq` build the dictionary set with `lit.comparator()` and call `contains`, so a row group whose dictionary only holds `-0.0` gets skipped for `x = 0.0`. This is intentional, following `client-go` behavior: callers never wait for a reload. "Fresh" here only means "read less than one reload interval ago", not "valid". The held token was valid when read, and producers rotate tokens well before they expire (Kubernetes at 80% of the TTL). Returning only fresh tokens would mean making concurrent callers wait for the reload, which puts file I/O on every request's path, for no gain.

I think what might be confusing here is that we traverse the delta snapshots from latest to oldest. In that order we can check whether a file in the same range has been added + removed, which is the only problematic case for the non-ordered reader.

When we only ever add XOR remove a specific data file, there is no problem at all. When we add and then remove it in the same range, we will detect the removal first, emit the removal (which will remove nothing), and once we get to the add, we check whether we have already removed the data file and skip it entirely. That way we can emit the read requests with a single traversal of the snapshot chain.

body: I think the FieldStats test would best be in the adapter integration PR as that is the boundary which actually writes these bounds into FieldStats. I went ahead and duplicated both. My rationale for duplicate is that the adapter would only read the bounds, so we don't need a full copy, but duplicate costs almost nothing and means one bound can't be affected by reading the other. For example, with identity both bounds would be the same buffer, so if the adapter wrote the lower bound with a relative read, the upper bound would then be empty and get written as a too-small bound, causing files to be incorrectly pruned.

body: Updated so null partition values and non-order-preserving transforms both return null instead of throwing. For context, I originally wrote this utility with the intent that callers (specifically the adapter) would always check if the value is null and only call it for monotonic transforms, but that's really a choice about how we implement the adapter, and handling it here is clearer. I think returning null is better than returning `<null, null>` because when the partition value is null every source value is null, so there are no bounds at all. A null upper already means unbounded in PartitionSourceBounds, so `<null, null>` would mean "non-null values exist, but we don't know their range", which isn't true for an all-null partition. Callers would still have to special-case it to avoid reporting bounds for a column with no non-null values, so returning null makes that case explicit.

With `distZip` as the only unclassified artifact, Gradle derives the POM packaging from it, so the published POM should end with `<packaging>zip</packaging>` and no `-sources.jar` / `-javadoc.jar` alongside.
Central requires sources and javadoc jars for any packaging other than `pom`, and the close of the staging repository on repository.apache.org can reject it for that, which would block the RC.

Can you check the output of `generatePomFileForApachePublication` for this module?

Two ways to fix it:
- add `artifact sourceJar` and `artifact javadocJar` (both tasks are already created for this project above), or
- set `pom.packaging = 'pom'` and publish the zip with a classifier.

If the `hive` distribution is added here as @kevinjqliu suggested, a classified `hive` zip doesn't change this: the main zip remains the unclassified artifact.

Sorry for raising this so late. After some offline discussions, I’m wondering whether we should enforce `all entries for a given key must be in the same file` in the index spec, as this may be difficult to maintain for certain (admittedly more extreme) use cases. For a very common key that keeps receiving new entries, each new entry would require rewriting the region file to add another line, and at this point we will need to trade between:
- Higher rewrite costs: Each new entry for that key triggers another rewrite of the region file. To satisfy the same-file requirement, the file would keep growing, making each rewrite increasingly expensive.
- Lower index usability: Updating the index less frequently to allow the rewrite to catch up/keep rewrite costs manageable would make the index less likely to be up to date, and therefore less usable for non-time-travel queries.

On the other hand, if we allow entries for a given key to span multiple region files, I think we could avoid this tradeoff by splitting those entries across more files whenever needed.

body:
Thanks, this is a valid concern for hot keys.

The main target is keys that are almost unique, like primary keys, where duplicates are rare. For these, the same-file rule costs nothing, and a lookup reads exactly one region file.

Allowing a key to span multiple region files would change the read path in two ways:
- If the matched `max_ordering_key` equals the key, the reader also has to check the next tracking file entry. This is a small cost.
- A lookup may need to read an unbounded range of region files instead of one. That is a structural change, and may need a scan-like plan instead of a single file read.

Indexes with hot keys can already get this flexibility by ending the ordering key with a unique field, like `[ bucket(256, user_id), user_id, _row_id ]`. Region boundaries can then split a hot key, and lookups prune on the ordering key prefix. New rows get increasing row IDs, so a refresh rewrites at most the last region file of the key. This way only these indexes pay for multi-file lookups.

I left this as a comment in another thread, but expire snapshots is a different beast from all the other actions. It's about removing history, and to accomplish that the only thing we *really* need to do is erase the snapshots from the metadata.json file. The other part of the action, cleaning up files, is not really critical to success. If we don't clean up some files that we otherwise should have, it's not a huge deal.

So basically we're doing the same thing here we were always doing: if we find some file we're supposed to delete and it's not there, we log a warning and move on.

For every other action, failing to read a manifest means the table is corrupted. If I try to rewrite a table or its manifests and a manifest isn't there, that's a failure, and a "partial success" still leaves us with a corrupt table. Orphan removal is even worse: it uses the manifests of live snapshots to decide what's still referenced, so skipping a missing manifest would make its data files look like orphans and we'd delete them. That turns a repairable table into permanent data loss. This is also why the valid-files side of expire stays strict in this PR.

So I'd keep `SkipMissingManifest` private to […]

body:
Taking a step back, here is my motivation for the refactor: I found that in terms of encryption support, our readers are asymmetric now, e.g. Spark readers can read encrypted data and deletes files, but `GenericReader` and `IcebergInputFormat` can't read encrypted delete files, while `EqualityConvertReader` can't read neither encrypted data nor delete files. The idea is to wire-in `InputFilesDecryptor` into the readers where we get it guaranteed that given a `ScanTask` by the reader we have all the referenced files involved with decryption, eliminating asymmetry.
Other motivation is that whenever we add new set of files, e.g. ColumnFiles into the picture, we don't forget to implement encryption support for them. Doing that in `InputFilesDecryptor` solves this too.

The above proposal makes `referencedFiles` in Spark redundant with what `InputFilesDecryptor` is meant to do.

The goal is to allow more general column replacements by making writers avoid ambiguous situations. Unlike my earlier rules, this requires writers to be more aware of exactly which values they are overwriting, but it allows more generic replacement.

The key rule we are trying to respect is:

"Listing a nested field does not change whether its parent struct is null. To change that, the column file must list the parent struct."

3. An added column file must list:

i think mostly looks good (use minor great-arc between endpoints for the SPHERICAL edge interpolation), but can you explain the rationale for some of the impl decisions?

- Arc-containment checks use a 1e-12 tolerance.
- Cross-product lengths at or below 1e-6 trigger conservative handling: nearly antipodal endpoints produce world bounds; short arcs get latitude padding based on their angular length.
- Computed latitude extrema are widened outward by the larger of 1e-6° or a 1e-7 relative margin, clamped to ±90°.
- Longitude coverage follows the shorter circular interval (the shorter one around the world), representing antimeridian crossings with west > east. Computed bounds reaching a pole expand to all longitudes.

body:
Good catch, min/med/max on a driver-side value just repeat the total, which isn't useful.

I looked at moving it to `currentMetricsValues()`. In Spark 4.1, `WritingSparkTask` collects the task metrics once, right before it calls `DataWriter.commit()`, and our `commit()` is where the writer gets closed and the buffered rows are flushed. So there are basically two options:

1. Keep it on the driver (what the PR does now). The write and close totals are both accurate, but min/med/max show the total.
2. Report `writeDuration` from the tasks through `currentMetricsValues()`. That gives a real min/med/max, but only for the row-level write calls. The close time can't be a task metric, so it still goes through the commit messages with only a total. For files smaller than a row group I think most of the actual I/O happens in that close, so the per-task numbers could understate the slow tasks.

Neither is great. What do you think, would you prefer one of these, or is there another way you'd go about it?

body:
This `finally` covers the failure behind the timeouts. On 2.2 and 2.3, `StreamTask.cleanUp` calls `disableInterruptOnCancel()` and `Thread.interrupted()` before `resourceCloser.close()`, where `closeAllOperators` is registered, so cancellation can't interrupt `awaitTermination` inside `close()`. The double close can only come from `processWatermark` leaving a closed service behind.

Only 2.2 and 2.3 hang, although #18815 backported `testConvertEqualityDeletesWithRewriteEnabledE2e` to 1.20 as well. Since 2.2, `Task.doRun` closes `invokable.cleanUp` inside its failure handler, so an exception from `close()` ends in "FATAL - exception in exception handler of task" and stops the only TaskManager, while 1.20 adds it as a suppressed exception. The 2.2 tree has hit the same timeout on main since Nov 9, so it needs this fix too.

CREATE MATERIALIZED VIEW event_agg_30_day_mv

body:
Following some research and implementation feedback from https://github.com/apache/iceberg/pull/18676/changes, I’m leaning toward keeping `vector(E, D)` as an Iceberg primitive.

The implementation in [#18676](https://github.com/apache/iceberg/pull/18676) strengthens that preference. `VectorType` fits into the existing primitive-type machinery, with `E` and `D` as type parameters and the existing schema serialization path handling the type. A vector field has its normal field ID, with no additional element field ID. This seems natural for a single schema value, similar to `fixed(L)`.

Other databases provide precedents for both approaches:

- Oracle explicitly classifies VECTOR as a [scalar type family in PL/SQL](https://docs.oracle.com/en/database/oracle/oracle-database/26/lnpls/sql-data-types.html).
- [pgvector defines vector as a PostgreSQL base type](https://github.com/pgvector/pgvector/blob/master/sql/vector.sql), which PostgreSQL describes as a [base/scalar type](https://www.postgresql.org/docs/current/sql-createtype.html#SQL-CREATETYPE-BASETYPE).
- Cassandra includes VECTOR among [native types](https://cassandra.apache.org/doc/stable/cassandra/developing/cql/types.html), sep […]

body:
Thanks for the fast response!

I think appending `_row_id` is a useful strategy, though:
- The strategy must be chosen at index creation: Since the ordering key is immutable, an existing index cannot adopt this optimization without creating a replacement index. If unexpected skew later makes splitting necessary to keep maintenance viable, the index would violate the proposed same-file requirement by doing so. My concern is making that adaptation depend on an upfront definition choice which is not that easy to predict.
- The maintenance problem arises well before unbounded read fanout: A lookup spanning an unbounded number of index files is a valid worst-case concern. But a more moderate case is a key receiving enough new entries that repeatedly rewriting its region prevents maintenance from keeping up. Splitting those entries across a few files could make updates manageable while still providing a substantial benefit over scanning the source table. The single-file guarantee therefore imposes a concrete maintenance cost even where multi-file lookups would remain useful.

body:
Another confirmation of this leak. In our case the trigger was an S3 write failure while the task's writers were being closed (`SinkWriter.close()` → "Failed to close partitioned delta writer"); the write failure itself was a permissions issue on our side. The task was killed, but its coordinator thread kept running in the Connect worker JVM with the old catalog, attempting a commit every cycle on its own schedule regardless of task restarts. Only restarting the worker clears it.

#18909 fixes the leak, not the write failure: `CommitterImpl.close()` now stops the coordinator even when stopping the worker throws, and still rethrows the original error. Any failure in `stopWorker()` (network, storage, permissions) no longer leaves a coordinator behind.

Relation to #18039: fencing ends a leaked coordinator once a new coordinator starts and the old one makes its next transactional write. It doesn't prevent the leak, so if the connector stays failed, is paused, or is deleted, the thread and its Kafka clients and catalog keep running until the worker restarts. The two changes are complementary.

body: Thanks @pvary for taking a look and the comment. Sharing is the better direction, and Hive already does it: CachedClientPool is a static cache. For the other catalogs it isn't the case today. A RESTSessionCatalog creates its own HTTPClient with a connection pool, auth session, FileIO and a one-thread rest-metrics-reporter pool per instance, and JdbcCatalog creates its own JdbcClientPool. All of these are released only by close(), which is why BaseMetastoreCatalog, RESTCatalog and InMemoryCatalog are Closeable. The static Flink sink already closes its catalog (TableLoader), and so does Kafka Connect (IcebergSinkTask). The dynamic sink operators are the exception: each loads a catalog from the CatalogLoader and never closes it. This only aligns them, and it wouldn't get in the way of pooling later. Previously this was deterministic: expiry was unknown for opaque tokens, so the retry always repeated the normal exchange (hence `times(2)`).

Now the outcome depends on whether the retry (100ms + 0–9ms jitter) lands after the 1s expiry, and the margin is only a few ms, since the refresh is scheduled ~100ms before expiry.

Not per sign request, but per `FileIO` instance. And we could have hundreds if not thousands of those in the same JVM.

A freshly-created Caffeine cache cost little memory, but if the cache is per `FileIO`, this means that 2 `FileIO`s belonging to the same principal cannot share the cache, which results in more calls to the sign endpoint than necessary.

Instead, I would keep the cache static, but would change the cache key.

But adding `token` or `client:secret` only to the cache key is not enough. Other auth managers may include other types of credentials, and since 1.12, catalog servers can also send credential-like data in the `remote-signing-config` object: these should be part of the cache key as well. As an extra protection, I think that the endpoint URI should also be part of the cache key.

In conclusion, the cache key should include the whole `properties()` map. Two clients with identical properties are indistinguishable to any signing server, and can safely keep sharing cache entries. The signing endpoint, the credentials and the remote signing configuration are all derived from them, and are thus included automatically.

Including the whole properties map doesn't hurt t […]

Keeping this PR open; status update.

This is a reference implementation of the index spec (#16961). The spec has been revised substantially since this PR was based on it (most recently on Nov 9), so the on-disk format here follows an earlier draft of the spec. I plan to realign the metadata, tracking-file and region-file layers with the spec once it settles, rather than chasing each revision.

Separately, I have continued the engine side on a Spark 4.0 branch (not part of this PR): https://github.com/osscm/iceberg/tree/scalar_sec_index_spark40 . It adds a resolver extracted from the scan builder, driver-side caching of index metadata, and handling for lookups that match nothing (an empty result prunes the scan instead of falling back to a full scan), plus a benchmark harness.

cc @huaxingao @pvary

body:
Thanks for the review! This is still decided by field id. The loop goes through each field id in the old schema and looks up the same id in the new schema. Since field ids never change, an id is missing from the new schema only when that field, or a parent of that field, was dropped. So the result is deterministic, and the only new entries are the fields nested under a dropped or renamed column.

Agreed that these properties are only meaningful for leaf columns. That is why this change is needed. For example, with `location struct<lat, long>` and a property on `location.lat`, `deleteColumn("location")` used to only look at `location` itself, so the property on the leaf `location.lat` was left behind. The new code includes the leaf columns, so it is removed. List element and map key/value paths work the same way, e.g. a property on `points.element.x` is removed when `points` is dropped.

Non-leaf names like `location` or `points.element` are also in the list, but they don't match any property, so they have no effect.

body:
I wonder what the level of knowledge such a `RootManifestFile` should contain. For me this seems a simple abstraction that holds a couple of fields like location, length, etc.
However, we now move knowledge about location resolution, FileIO, an entire `Snapshot` object here, and if I'm not mistaken also encryption related knowledge about how to get `keyMetadata` from `keyId` (or from the new fields we potentially add).
I think such a knowledge should live one abstraction level above and `RootManifestFile` should have a single constructor accepting the pre-computed values. If we have multiple places where we create `RootManifestFile`s then maybe we should construct them either from `Snapshot`, or from some class like we have for `DataFiles`.
WDYT?
